soil-fert-228.title: Chlorosis, when green leaves fade to yellow
soil-fert-228.text: A pale leaf belongs to a plant short of food. Chlorosis is the condition in which leaves make too little chlorophyll and turn pale, yellow or yellow-white. Such a plant makes little carbohydrate by photosynthesis and may die unless the cause is treated. Causes include soil shortages of iron, magnesium, zinc or nitrogen, a soil pH that locks up minerals, waterlogging and damaged or compacted roots. On French limestone vineyards, grafting vines onto American rootstocks after phylloxera worsened this lime chlorosis. Remedies match the cause: iron chelate or sulfate, magnesium or nitrogen feeds, lime on acid soils and sulfur on alkaline ones.

soil-fert-231.title: Nitrogen deficiency and the sawdust that robs it
soil-fert-231.text: Sawdust dug into a garden can starve the plants it was meant to help. Soil organisms feeding on such high-carbon matter use up the available nitrogen, 'robbing' it from roots. The result is nitrogen deficiency: stunted plants, poor flowering and fruiting, and chlorosis. Older leaves yellow first, because the plant moves nitrogen to younger tissue. Other stresses mimic these signs, so soil and tissue tests or chlorophyll meters confirm it, since leaf nitrogen tracks chlorophyll. Crops grown over winter and plowed under, as in {{ref:soil-fert-026}}, limit leaching, and leguminous ones fix extra nitrogen. Feeds such as ammonium phosphate correct it.

soil-fert-238.title: Mitscherlich's curve of diminishing yield
soil-fert-238.text: In 1909 Alexander Mitscherlich gave the harvest a curve. His law of physiological relations ties yield to the quantity of plant food through a logarithmic function, so each added dose brings a smaller gain. It recast the limiting-factor idea that Liebig had framed as {{ref:soil-fert-182}} and that Blackman later discussed. When the two were compared in 1942, Mitscherlich's function proved to be virtually the law of diminishing returns.

soil-fert-229.title: Manganese deficiency and the checkered young leaf
soil-fert-229.text: A four-manganese core drives the oxygen-evolving complex of photosystem II, the heart of photosynthesis. That is why most broad-spectrum fertilizers contain manganese. Manganese deficiency is commonest in poorly drained soils and where organic matter is high, and at high pH the metal may be unavailable. Leaves yellow between the veins in a checkered pattern. Young leaves show it first, because manganese is immobile in the plant, unlike magnesium. It is often confused with {{ref:soil-fert-201}}, and the two occur together. Ammonium sulfate lowers pH at once; sulfur works slowly through soil bacteria. The US used about 20,000 tons of manganese fertilizer compounds in 2000.

soil-fert-226.title: Boron deficiency, the world's commonest micronutrient gap
soil-fert-226.text: No micronutrient shortage is more widespread in crops than boron deficiency. Without boron, cells stop expanding, growing points die and fertility falls. Soils typically hold an adequate 0.5 to 1.0 mg/kg; below 0.2 to 0.5 mg/kg, depending on crop and soil, deficiency is common. High-pH soils are prone, because boric acid stays undissociated there and roots cannot absorb it. So are soils under 1.5% organic matter and leached sandy soils. In calcareous fields in Pakistan, 35 to 56 percent are deficient. Boric acid, borax or Solubor at about 1.1 kg boron per hectare corrects it, but excess is toxic.

soil-fert-232.title: Phosphorus deficiency and the purple warning
soil-fert-232.text: Most of the phosphorus in a soil sits in forms plants cannot absorb. Plants take it up as phosphate ions, and soil pH sets which forms of phosphate exist; between pH 6 and 7 the least is bound up. Phosphorus deficiency slows maturity and makes plants store excess starch. Some turn dark purple from anthocyanin, a pigment, but only once the shortage is fairly severe. Soil tests such as Bray 1-P, Mehlich 3 and Olsen extract phosphorus for colorimetric measurement. Roots fight back by favoring lateral roots and secreting phosphatases and organic acids. Larger roots and mycorrhizal partners raise uptake.

soil-fert-233.title: Potassium deficiency and the scorched leaf tip
soil-fert-233.text: Potassium slips easily out of light, sandy soils. With little clay to hold it, the soluble nutrient leaches away, and potassium deficiency, also called potash deficiency, follows. Leaf tips scorch brown and curl, with yellowing between the veins. Older leaves show it first, because potassium is mobile in the plant. Deficient plants suffer more from frost and disease, though potassium above the optimum adds no extra resistance. Potassium chloride is the main remedy. Dry soil cuts uptake, while adding lime or raising organic matter can improve retention.

soil-fert-230.title: Zinc deficiency, from cereal fields to dinner plates
soil-fert-230.text: Almost half the world's cereal crops grow on zinc-deficient soils, so zinc deficiency is widespread in people too. In plants it means limited growth, because roots cannot take up enough of this essential micronutrient. Some soils hold little zinc, such as sandy soils and highly weathered soils. Others, such as calcareous and saline soils, bind it tightly to their particles. Low organic matter and compaction add risk. Phosphorus fertilizers and lime frequently induce it, lime by increasing that binding. Leaf zinc of 20 to 100 mg/kg suffices for most crops. Zinc sulfate or oxide at 5 to 100 kg/ha corrects it, though perhaps not in alkaline soils.

soil-fert-235.title: Nitrogen use efficiency: the share a crop actually uses
soil-fert-235.text: Crops worldwide generally absorb less than half the nitrogen offered to them. Nitrogen use efficiency is the proportion of the nitrogen present that a plant absorbs and uses, and for most crops it falls below 50%. Raising it cuts fertilizer runoff and production costs while increasing yield, making farming more sustainable. Better fertilizers and crop management help, as do selective breeding and genetic engineering. Efficiency can be measured for the plant, the soil, the fertilizer or the whole ecosystem.

soil-fert-227.title: Calcium deficiency, a problem of water more than soil
soil-fert-227.text: Blossom end rot in tomatoes and peppers, bitter pit in stored apples and tipburn in lettuce share one cause. Calcium deficiency comes from too little available calcium or, more often, from low transpiration of the plant or the affected tissue. Calcium does not move in the phloem, so low-transpiring tissues and new, fast-growing parts suffer first. Acidic, sandy or coarse soils often hold less calcium, and high-phosphorus soils tend to lock it into insoluble forms. Adding lime to acid soils toward pH 6.5 can help. Adding calcium at the roots seldom cures it, so steady watering is key.

soil-fert-234.title: Hoagland solution, the standard recipe for soilless plants
soil-fert-234.text: More than 21,000 citations point to one recipe for feeding plants without soil. Hoagland and Snyder devised the Hoagland solution in 1933, a standard hydroponic nutrient solution that supplies every essential plant element. It was meant to imitate a nutrient-rich soil solution, and its high nitrogen and potassium suit large plants such as tomato and bell pepper. Revisions added ferric chelates to keep iron in solution. In 1938 the trace elements were cut to the accepted essentials: B, Mn, Zn, Cu, Mo, Fe and Cl. Arnon's 1950 revision changed only molybdenum, from 0.048 to 0.011 ppm.

soil-fert-236.title: Reading a leaf's nitrogen without picking it
soil-fert-236.text: A laboratory tissue test usually takes one to two weeks, and by then the time to act may have passed. Non-destructive tissue tests answer in the field. They estimate a crop's nitrogen status from leaf chlorophyll without destroying the sample. The link is chemical: each chlorophyll molecule contains four nitrogen atoms. Absorption meters shine light through a leaf. Brands report different units, such as SPAD, which convert, and readings are linear only below 300 mg/m2. Fluorescence-ratio meters read up to 675 mg/m2 and can measure small, curved or thick samples.

soil-fert-218.title: Biogeochemistry, the science of Earth as a living whole
soil-fert-218.text: Vladimir Vernadsky saw the Earth as a living whole. His 1926 book The Biosphere made that case, and he is called the founder of modern biogeochemistry. The field studies the chemical, physical, geological and biological processes that govern the make-up of the natural environment, the pedosphere included. At its center are the biogeochemical cycles of elements and their passage through living things, especially carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, sulfur, iron and phosphorus. Its roots reach back to eighteenth-century agricultural interest in soil chemistry, which improved the understanding of nutrients. An 1844 paper by Dumas and Boussingault counts as a milestone. A systems science close to systems ecology, it lives in many disciplines, from ecology, geology and oceanography to soil science. Research ranges from recovery after soil and water acidification to the carbon storage of {{ref:soil-env-212}}. Evolutionary biogeochemistry turns the same lens on Earth's geologic history and the evolution of life.

soil-fert-224.title: Urease, the enzyme that decides urea's fate
soil-fert-224.text: More than half of all synthetic nitrogen fertilizer is one compound, described in {{ref:soil-fert-021}}, and one enzyme decides how much of it is wasted. Urease, which contains nickel, breaks that compound down into carbon dioxide and ammonia. The reaction runs in two stages through carbamic acid, and the basic ammonia raises the pH around it. A key catalyst of the nitrogen cycle, urease occurs as a {{ref:soil-bio-039}}, likely because soil microbes gain from the ammonium it frees. Rapid breakdown wastes fertilizer, so inhibiting urease with chemicals such as NBPT is an agricultural goal. Its activity also serves as an indicator of the health of microbial communities.

soil-fert-221.title: Nitrospira, the bacterium that broke a nitrification rule
soil-fert-221.text: A long-held view said nitrification needs two organisms, one for each step. Nitrospira helped overturn it. This genus of bacteria oxidizes nitrite to nitrate, the second step, yet some members, such as Nitrospira inopinata, carry out both steps alone, as {{ref:soil-fert-110}} describes. First described in 1986 from the Gulf of Maine, it lives in forest soils, rice paddies and farmland as well as water systems and wastewater plants. It is hard to culture, so most knowledge of it comes from molecular and genomic data. Some make their own urease, and the ammonia it frees lets ammonia oxidizers live alongside them.

soil-fert-219.title: Leghemoglobin, the red guardian of the root nodule
soil-fert-219.text: Legume root nodules hold a red protein that closely resembles hemoglobin. This is leghemoglobin, an oxygen-carrying plant globin made only when rhizobia colonize the roots. It solves a dilemma. {{ref:soil-fert-101}} is oxygen-sensitive, yet energy-hungry nitrogen fixation needs respiration, and respiration needs oxygen. Leghemoglobin builds up to millimolar levels, keeping free oxygen in the nanomolar range while holding enough total oxygen. Plants need it for symbiotic fixation but not for growth when fixed nitrogen is supplied. Its main job is still debated. A 1995 study pointed to oxygen delivery; 2005 knockout studies found it both buffers and delivers oxygen.

soil-fert-222.title: The selenium cycle, a loop of give and take
soil-fert-222.text: Selenium moves through living things in a loop. Bacteria, fungi and plants, especially species of Astragalus, reduce its oxidized forms, selenate and selenite, to selenide; other organisms oxidize it back. On semi-arid seleniferous soils, rich in selenium, accumulator plants return organic selenium to the soil as they decay. Yet soil selenium there stays mainly inorganic, evidence that it is re-oxidized. In sediment, selenate reduced to selenite sticks to clay and reacts with iron, locking selenium away. Some organic forms escape as vapor from water, sediment or plants. Oxidation and methylation by roots and microorganisms return selenium to food chains.

soil-fert-223.title: Sulfur assimilation, from sulfate to cysteine
soil-fert-223.text: Plants spend energy to take up sulfur. Sulfur assimilation is how living things build sulfur into their molecules. In plants it begins at the root, which takes up sulfate actively at a cost in ATP. Uptake generally reaches its maximum rate at sulfate levels of 0.1 mM and lower. The transpiration stream carries sulfate to the shoot, where chloroplasts reduce it to sulfide and build it into cysteine, an amino acid. When sulfate runs short, most sulfate transporter genes are expressed up to 100-fold more strongly. Bacteria and fungi follow a similar route, reducing sulfate through APS and sulfite to sulfide for cysteine.

soil-fert-225.title: Nitrous oxide reductase, the last brake on a greenhouse gas
soil-fert-225.text: Nitrous oxide is a potent greenhouse gas, and one bacterial enzyme keeps much of it out of the air. Nitrous oxide reductase performs the last step of denitrification, reducing nitrous oxide to nitrogen gas. By consuming the gas inside cells, it greatly limits emissions to the atmosphere. Only denitrifying prokaryotes can make this conversion. Some communities do only this step, while some denitrifiers lack the enzyme and stop at nitrous oxide. Encoded by nos genes, it is a copper enzyme in the bacterial periplasm. Its catalytic CuZ site is a cluster of four copper atoms bound with sulfide. Acetylene is its most specific inhibitor.

soil-fert-220.title: Nitrogen-15 tracing: following one heavy atom
soil-fert-220.text: Soil ammonium can be made and used up at the same moment, so its concentration alone hides what is happening. Nitrogen-15 tracing follows the heavy stable isotope nitrogen-15 through the nitrogen cycle to measure each conversion. Natural-abundance methods need no disturbance; they express 15N as delta values relative to air. The 15N site preference within nitrous oxide helps tell nitrification from denitrification. Enrichment methods add 15N-labeled ammonium or nitrate, allowing precise rate calculations, though the added nitrogen can bias natural transformations. Rates of simultaneous processes are solved numerically, for example with the Ntrace model, based on a Markov chain Monte Carlo simulation.
